Yet he ran a palace bazaar—himself butchering, selling ale, and weighing coin.
Yet he ran a palace bazaar, having others butcher and sell ale while he weighed the goods himself with exact accuracy.
使人屠酤 assigns butchering and selling to other people; 手揣斤兩 says he personally gauged weights, not that he weighed coin.
He drew double stipends to bankroll favorites.
He habitually drew two months of the palace allowance in advance to supply his favorites.
探取二月 describes drawing two months in advance, not a doubling of the regular stipend.

He had not yet seen Your Highness and feared that drinking this would leave him incapacitated.
又未見殿下，飲此或至顛倒 refers to not yet seeing the addressee and fear of intoxication; it says nothing about copying a document.
Lü jailed and starved Yu; sympathizers smuggled food over walls.
Lü reported to Liu Zhen, who moved Yu to a small compound and cut off all food; palace sympathizers still passed food to him over the walls.
慮以告劉振，振乃徙 explicitly switches the acting subject from Sun Lü to Liu Zhen for moving and starving the prince.
She posed as hoping Yu could repent posthumously.
She claimed she had hoped Yu would take the lesson deeply to heart, reconsider his filial duty, and bow in repentance to restore his name.
The memorial recalls Jia’s claimed earlier hope for Yu to repent and rectify his standing; it does not claim that repentance could occur after his death.
Huguan's steadfast lord—autumn-thousand years awakened self.
The elder of Huguan remonstrated with his ruler; Qianqiu brought him to recognize his error.
壺關 and 千秋 are historical allusions, not a steadfast lord and autumn-thousand years. Pinned Hanshu073 s0031/s0062 and Hanshu077 s0072–77 establish the remonstrances and the emperor’s realization.
The elder of Huguan spoke up for the wronged prince; Qianqiu made the emperor see his error.
The parallel allusions concern remonstrance for the wronged Han crown prince. Exact pinned Hanshu witnesses are sealed separately; this restores the named Qianqiu instead of a generic summary.
